_comment: Kitchen answers to questions the Weekly Stock Check workbook cannot answer.
Every entry is something a person decided, not something a script derived,
so each one records who said it and when. The importer applies these on top
of the workbook and reports any that no longer match a catalog row.
base_unit      the unit the item is measured in, where the workbook tracks
neither a loose unit nor a unit count.
case           how a supplier's case breaks down. Either per_case plus
item_size and item_unit for a case of discrete things, or
case_size and case_unit for bulk sold by weight with no
countable item inside it.
needs_health_mark  whether the item's label carries the oval health mark.
It follows animal origin, so it sits on the raw meat and
bone ingredients rather than on the products made from
them. Anything absent from this file stays null, meaning
not yet determined rather than no mark.
An entry may also create an item the workbook does not have at all. Those
carry an explicit id, kind and base_unit, and their ids are prefixed
`trace:` so it is obvious at a glance which rows came from the workbook
and which this project minted.
locations and suppliers are listed here in full rather than derived: the
workbook records a storage word per ingredient and two sites, but never
which physical areas exist. Only Glasgow is in scope.
after_opening states how an item must be kept once opened. Dean's rule is
that it matches the unopened requirement everywhere except the items
listed as exceptions, which move to the fridge. The rule is applied only
where the unopened requirement is known, so products, which have none,
stay null on both.
product_storage covers the finished products, which the workbook records
no storage for at all. The frozen lines and the shelf-stable oils and
sauces are named; everything else goes to the walk-in fridge.
excluded lists rows that are in the workbook but out of scope at Glasgow.
They are imported as inactive rather than skipped: skipping them would
let the next import quietly add them back, and the catalog reads return
active rows only, so an inactive row is already invisible to a picker.

case.reason: sold per kg, so there is no fixed case size to convert from

item_suppliers._comment: Which supplier an ingredient comes from, where the kitchen's records could not say, and which pairings are an emergency backup rather than the normal source. Applied on top of the Goods In Records mapping.

opening._comment: What opening a pack does to it. Fifteen ingredients get a Date Opened label; every other ingredient is used whole and is marked whole_pack by the importer. Where the supplier's specification states a period it is used; where it does not, the kitchen's own six-week rule applies, which is tighter than the packs require and is the kitchen's decision rather than the supplier's (Dean, 2026-08-31).

decided._comment: Periods the kitchen set for these items specifically, rather than the blanket six-week rule. Salt and MSG keep far longer than the rule allows for and were moved to three months (Dean, 2026-09-01). Three months is recorded as 90 days, the same way the balsamic vinegar's supplier specification is.

product_units._comment: What a finished product is counted in (Dean, 2026-09-01). The P0 rule made every product Units, which is right for a packet of frozen ramen and wrong for a broth. Broths are counted in litres, soups in grams, and sauces, pastes and oils in kilograms packed two kilograms to a tub. Anything not named here keeps Units.

pack_sizes._comment: What one pack holds and how many come in a case (Dean, 2026-09-01). The workbook's Case Size column carries the size but never says what unit the number is in, and its LooseUnit column is empty for all of these, so the P0 rule counted them in Units while the recipes weigh them. These figures set the base unit and give the case -> pack -> base conversions.
pack_sizes._spring_onion: Spring Onion is 12 bunches to a case and the recipes use it in grams, but nobody has weighed a bunch. It stays counted in bunches and its recipe line stays unconvertible until somebody does — a made-up bunch weight would make every yield using it wrong.
